content.summary: Read about a film made with a small budget and compare it with a big studio production. You will practise finding the main idea and important details, while noticing how writers compare films, people, and actions.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use -er or more to compare two things, and -est or the most to compare three or more. Use (not) as...as to show that things are similar or different. Comparative adverbs describe how actions are done, for example, more carefully or faster.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words for films, film-making, money, people in shows, and entertainment.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the passage first to understand its main idea. Then scan for names, numbers, and comparisons that answer specific questions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short text about making a film.
Locate details about a film's budget, production, and success.
Recognize comparative and superlative adjectives, (not) as...as, and comparative adverbs in context.

contextWarmup.prompt: A small film company has less money than a big studio. What might help its film look professional?
options: Careful planning and creative ideas
A more expensive ticket
A longer list of contestants
contextWarmup.explanation: Careful planning and creative ideas can help a small team make a good film without spending more money.

rules: For many short adjectives, add -er to compare two things and -est to compare three or more: cheap, cheaper, the cheapest. Use than after a comparative when you name the second thing.
For many longer adjectives, use more to compare and the most to show the highest degree: more expensive, the most expensive.
Use not as + adjective + as to say that two things are different: The film is not as long as the original.
Use a lot, much, or far to make a comparison stronger, and a little or a bit to make it weaker: The second version is a little shorter.
To compare actions, use a comparative adverb. Many adverbs use more + adverb, as in more carefully. Some are irregular: fast becomes faster, good becomes better, and badly becomes worse.

commonTrap.explanation: Do not use more and -er together for the same adjective. Also check whether you are comparing an adjective or describing how someone does something.
commonTrap.wrong: The film is more cheaper than the other one.
commonTrap.correct: The film is cheaper than the other one. For an action, say: The team worked more carefully.

content.passageTitle: A Small Film with Big Ideas
paragraphs: When Maya's film club decided to make a movie, they had a budget of just £600. That was far less than the cost of a big studio film. The club chose a funny story about a school talent show, so they did not need expensive locations or special effects. Maya thought a short film would be easier to finish than a full-length movie.

The students planned each scene carefully and borrowed a camera from their school. They also asked teachers to act and invited friends to be extras. The actors worked more patiently than they expected, and the club made the film a little shorter after watching the first version. It was not as polished as a Hollywood production, but it looked nearly as professional as some films made with much bigger budgets. At a local festival, it won the prize for the most successful student film. Maya says that good teamwork can be more important than expensive equipment.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Comparing Movies and Entertainment

content.summary: Practical guide on writing comparisons in English using comparative adjectives, superlative adjectives, equality structures, and comparative adverbs for entertainment reviews.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Comparative Adjectives Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + Short Adjective-er + than + Noun / Long Adjective (more + adjective) + than
blueprintItems.example: Digital video is cheaper and more convenient than 35mm film.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Superlative Adjectives Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + the + Short Adjective-est / the most + Long Adjective + in/of + Group
blueprintItems.example: Monsters was one of the best and the most exciting films of the year.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Modifying Comparisons Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + Intensifier (a lot / much / a little) + Comparative Adjective + than
blueprintItems.example: Independent movies are a lot more interesting than big studio blockbusters.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize movie titles, proper names, and the first word of every sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: monsters was one of the best films on netflix.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Monsters was one of the best films on Netflix.
mechanicsRules.why: Movie titles and streaming platforms are proper nouns and require capital letters in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'than' when comparing two specific things with a comparative adjective.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Action films are more exciting digital videos.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Action films are more exciting than digital videos.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'than' connects the two items being compared in a comparative sentence.

mechanicsRules.rule: Include the definite article 'the' before superlative adjectives.
mechanicsRules.badExample: This is most expensive ticket in the cinema.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: This is the most expensive ticket in the cinema.
mechanicsRules.why: Superlatives identify a unique item in a group, so they always require 'the'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the comparative form of the adjective in brackets:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Digital video is cheap compared to traditional film. [cheap]
practicumQuestions.hint: Add '-er' to short adjectives and use 'than'.
targetAnswers: Digital video is cheaper than traditional film.
Digital video is cheaper than traditional film
practicumQuestions.explanation: Short adjectives like 'cheap' take '-er' in the comparative form, followed by 'than'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the superlative form of the adjective in brackets:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Monsters was a good film of the year. [good]
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'the' and the irregular superlative form of 'good'.
targetAnswers: Monsters was the best film of the year.
Monsters was the best film of the year
practicumQuestions.explanation: The adjective 'good' is irregular. Its superlative form is 'the best'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Identify and fix the mistake in this comparative sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Action films are more exciting digital videos.
practicumQuestions.hint: What word is missing before 'digital videos'?
targetAnswers: Action films are more exciting than digital videos.
Action films are more exciting than digital videos
practicumQuestions.explanation: Comparatives require 'than' to connect the two items being compared.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite this sentence using the (not) as...as structure to show they have equal cost:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Ticket A and Ticket B cost the exact same amount. [expensive]
targetAnswers: Ticket A is as expensive as Ticket B.
Ticket A is as expensive as Ticket B
practicumQuestions.explanation: To show equality, use 'as + adjective + as'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: avatar was the most amazing movie on netflix.
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize proper nouns like movie titles and streaming platforms.
targetAnswers: Avatar was the most amazing movie on Netflix.
Avatar was the most amazing movie on Netflix
practicumQuestions.explanation: Both movie titles ('Avatar') and brand names ('Netflix') must be capitalized.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Make this comparison stronger using the intensifier 'much':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Independent movies are more interesting than Hollywood blockbusters.
practicumQuestions.hint: Insert 'much' right before the comparative adjective 'more'.
targetAnswers: Independent movies are much more interesting than Hollywood blockbusters.
Independent movies are much more interesting than Hollywood blockbusters
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intensifiers like 'much' or 'a lot' go before the comparative adjective to strengthen the claim.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform the sentence using the comparative form of the adverb in brackets:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The young actor spoke quietly during the rehearsal. [quietly]
targetAnswers: The young actor spoke more quietly during the rehearsal.
The young actor spoke more quietly during the rehearsal
practicumQuestions.explanation: Most adverbs ending in '-ly' form their comparatives by adding 'more' before the adverb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a comparative sentence about two genres of music (e.g., rock and pop) using the adjective 'energetic':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Compare rock music and pop music using 'energetic'.
practicumQuestions.hint: Rock music is more energetic than pop music.
targetAnswers: Rock music is more energetic than pop music.
Rock music is more energetic than pop music
practicumQuestions.explanation: Long adjectives like 'energetic' take 'more' in the comparative form.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the error in this superlative sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: This is most expensive ticket in the cinema.
practicumQuestions.hint: Superlatives need an article before them.
targetAnswers: This is the most expensive ticket in the cinema.
This is the most expensive ticket in the cinema
practicumQuestions.explanation: Superlative adjectives always require the definite article 'the'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Make this comparison weaker using the modifier 'a bit':
practicumQuestions.promptText: My video project was shorter than yours.
practicumQuestions.hint: Insert 'a bit' before the comparative adjective.
targetAnswers: My video project was a bit shorter than yours.
My video project was a bit shorter than yours
practicumQuestions.explanation: Modifiers like 'a bit' or 'a little' precede the comparative adjective to soften the difference.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Entertainment, Movies, and Comparisons

content.summary: This speaking module focuses on clear articulation when comparing movies, budgets, and forms of entertainment. You will practice linking comparative adjectives and using natural sentence stress to sound confident and fluent.
content.audioGuidance: Pay attention to sentence stress when making comparisons. Emphasize the comparative word, such as more, less, or the suffix -er, while keeping unstressed words like as or than quiet and fast.

pillars.name: Comparative Stress
pillars.target: Stress the key comparative word in a sentence
pillars.explanation: When you say 'more expensive' or 'better than', put stronger vocal weight on 'more', 'bett-', and the main adjective to make your comparison clear.

pillars.name: Schwa Reduction in Comparisons
pillars.target: Reduce the word 'than' to weak schwa sound
pillars.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce 'than' with a strong vowel. They say /ðən/ quickly, linking it smoothly to the preceding adjective.

pillars.name: Intonation in Opinions
pillars.target: Use rising and falling tones to express preferences
pillars.explanation: Use a slight rise when listing entertainment options and a clear fall at the end of your sentence when stating your final verdict or superlativeness.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The primary stress remains on the second syllable of expensive. The preceding word 'more' gets a medium secondary beat.
Notice that the primary stress stays on the second syllable of successful.
Stress the first syllable of budget clearly while emphasizing the comparative adjective.
Maintain the stress on the second syllable of exciting when using the modifier less.

drills.targetText: Hollywood films are much more expensive than independent movies.
drills.phonetic: /ˈhɒlɪwʊd fɪlmz ɑː mʌtʃ mɔːr ɪkˈspensɪv ðæn ˌɪndɪˈpendənt ˈmuːviz/
drills.focus: Comparative structures and weak pronunciation of 'than'
drills.hint: Link 'more' and 'expensive' together, and pronounce 'than' as a quick schwa sound.

drills.targetText: This animated film has a bigger budget than the last one.
drills.phonetic: /ðɪs ˈænɪmeɪtɪd fɪlm hæz ə ˈbɪɡə ˈbʌdʒɪt ðæn ðə lɑːst wʌn/
drills.hint: Make sure to link the 'r' sound in 'bigger' smoothly into 'budget'.

drills.targetText: Game show contestants can win ten thousand pounds.
drills.phonetic: /ɡeɪm ʃəʊ kənˈtestənts kæn wɪn ten ˈθaʊzənd paʊndz/
drills.hint: Articulate the final /ts/ in contestants cleanly.

drills.targetText: Skiing is not as exciting as playing football.
drills.phonetic: /ˈskiːɪŋ ɪz nɒt æz ɪkˈsaɪtɪŋ æz ˈpleɪɪŋ ˈfʊtbɔːl/
drills.hint: Pronounce 'as' with a weak form /əz/ in the middle of the sentence.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Speak fluently in full sentences using comparative structures.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about forms of entertainment you enjoy.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Compare watching animated films with playing video games. Which one do you prefer and why?
storyPoints: Mention both animated films and video games
Use the structure not as...as to compare them
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Watching animated films is not as exciting as playing video games with my friends.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈwɒtʃɪŋ ˈænɪmeɪtɪd fɪlmz ɪz nɒt æz ɪkˈsaɪtɪŋ æz ˈpleɪɪŋ ˈvɪdiəʊ ɡeɪmz wɪð maɪ frendz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure you use the target negative comparison structure accurately.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Listen to the prompt and respond as a movie fan talking to a ticket seller.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to the cinema! Are you looking for tickets to the new Hollywood blockbuster or the animated comedy?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Buying cinema tickets at the box office and choosing between two different films.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I want two tickets for the animated comedy because it has funnier characters.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Respond promptly using comparative adjectives to make your choice.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Listen to your friend and discuss movie budgets and film extras.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Did you know that some films have hundreds of extras and cost millions of dollars?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Discussing film production costs and Hollywood budgets with a friend.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, but films with a smaller budget can sometimes be more successful.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use comparative forms correctly in conversation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Talk about game show contestants and prizes with a classmate.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Would you ever want to be a contestant on a television game show to win ten thousand pounds?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Talking about TV game shows and winning prizes.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I would love to be a contestant because winning money is very exciting.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Keep your tone enthusiastic and conversational.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Compare professional actors with extras in a movie scene.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: What do you think is harder, being a professional actor with speaking lines or being an extra?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Debating film roles with a fellow student.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Being a professional actor is much more difficult than being an extra.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use comparative adjectives to contrast job difficulties.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the target sentence focusing on entertainment vocabulary.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence clearly: The successful film had a massive budget and professional actors.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The successful film had a massive budget and professional actors.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə səkˈsesfl fɪlm hæd ə ˈmæsɪv ˈbʌdʒɪt ənd prəˈfeʃənl ˈæktəz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Pronounce each vocabulary item with correct syllable stress.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the comparative grammar structure correctly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence clearly: Independent movies are often cheaper than Hollywood productions.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Independent movies are often cheaper than Hollywood productions.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˌɪndɪˈpendənt ˈmuːviz ɑːr ˈɒfn ˈtʃiːpə ðæn ˈhɒlɪwʊd prəˈdʌkʃnz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure the comparative suffix -er is clearly articulated followed by weak 'than'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Focus on syllable stress in multi-syllable entertainment words.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this sentence aloud, emphasizing the correct syllable stress in expensive and animated: That expensive animated film was fantastic.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: That expensive animated film was fantastic.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place primary stress on the second syllable of ex-PEN-sive and the first syllable of AN-i-ma-ted.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice rising and falling intonation when offering choices and giving conclusions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this sentence with a rising tone on the first option and a falling tone at the end: Do you prefer action movies, or do you prefer comedies?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Do you prefer action movies, or do you prefer comedies?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /duː juː prɪˈfɜːr ˈækʃn ˈmuːviz ɔː duː juː prɪˈfɜːr ˈkɒmədiz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a rising pitch on 'action movies' to show an open choice, and a falling pitch on 'comedies' to finish the question.
